sections.heading: Facing the day without pretending I am strong
sections.text: Lord of grace, the day is in front of me, and so is the world with all its pressure, noise, and temptation. I do not want to pretend I am braver or steadier than I am. I am weak, and I can be afraid. If I try to walk through today on my own, I will trip over myself. So I look to you for strength. Hold me close to your beloved Son, because in him I can stand when I would otherwise fall.
theological_themes: Human weakness before the pressures of the world
Dependence on God rather than self-confidence

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that his people bear fruit only by abiding in him, and that apart from him they can do nothing. This directly supports the prayer’s refusal to face the day in self-reliance.
Paul learns that Christ’s power is displayed in weakness, not in human strength. The section echoes that posture: honest weakness becoming the place where God’s strength is sought.

sections.heading: Asking you to keep me from myself
sections.text: Father, my own heart can betray me. If you leave me to myself, I will find ways to dishonor your name. So please open my eyes, lead me, and hold me up by your Spirit. Be the strength that keeps me standing, the light that helps me see clearly, the steady feet that help me obey, the protection around me, the weapon against evil, and the warmth that keeps my heart from growing cold. Make my life today bring you honor.
theological_themes: The treachery of the sinful heart
The Holy Spirit’s guidance, illumination, and sustaining power
God’s glory as the aim of daily obedience

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the Spirit as the one by whom believers put sin to death and are led as God’s children. This grounds the prayer’s request to be guided and upheld rather than ruled by the sinful heart.
God’s word is pictured as light for the path, which fits the prayer’s desire to see and walk rightly. The section asks God to give practical direction for faithful obedience.
Paul calls believers to stand in the Lord’s strength and use God-given armor against evil. This supports the prayer’s language of needing protection and a weapon in spiritual conflict.

sections.heading: Coming to your fullness with empty hands
sections.text: You do not become poorer by giving to me. Your mercy is not running low. Everything I need from you is found in your Son. So I come with empty hands, trusting Jesus. I do not bring you my record, my effort, or my excuses. I bring you Christ by faith, and I ask you to receive me because of him—the one who died for me and is enough for me.
theological_themes: Faith as receiving and resting on Christ rather than presenting personal merit

scripture_references.connection: John speaks of believers receiving grace from Christ’s fullness. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God’s giving does not diminish his abundance.
Paul says the fullness of deity dwells in Christ and that believers have been filled in him. The section’s claim that everything needed is found in the Son rests on this truth.
Paul argues that the Father who gave his Son will also graciously give what his people need. This grounds the prayer’s boldness in asking from God’s fullness through Christ.

sections.heading: Resting my whole case on Jesus
sections.text: Lord, I owe more than I can ever repay. My wrongs are real, and I have no way to settle the debt. So I plead the blood of Jesus—not as if I have to persuade you to be merciful, but because you yourself gave him for sinners like me. Let his worth stand in place of my unworthiness. Let his sinless life answer for my sin, his purity for my uncleanness, his honesty for my hidden deceit, his truth for my lies, his humility for my pride, his steadiness for my wandering, his love for my resistance, his fullness for my emptiness, his faithfulness for my betrayal, his obedience for my lawlessness, his honor for my shame, his devotion for my wayward heart, his holiness for my impurity, his righteousness for my dead works, and his death for the life I forfeited. I have no hope apart from him. In him, receive me, forgive me, and make me yours today.
theological_themes: Justification by Christ’s righteousness rather than human merit
Confession of sin in concrete moral terms
Faith pleading what God has provided in the gospel

scripture_references.connection: Paul states the great exchange: Christ, though sinless, is made sin for us so that in him we become the righteousness of God. This is the clearest foundation for the section’s series of Christ’s righteousness standing in place of the sinner’s guilt.

This passage holds together universal guilt, justification by grace, redemption in Christ, and his blood as the means God provided. It supports the prayer’s appeal to Christ’s blood as the answer to real moral debt.

Hebrews says Christ’s blood purifies the conscience from dead works to serve the living God. That directly relates to the prayer’s request for Christ’s righteousness in place of dead works and uncleanness.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly reflects Protestant doctrines of substitutionary atonement and imputed righteousness, which are central to its logic but are doctrinally contested in some Christian traditions.

The phrase about pleading Christ’s blood can sound, in modern ears, as though the sinner must persuade a reluctant Father. The adaptation keeps the legal and sacrificial appeal but clarifies that Christ is God’s own merciful provision.

The original’s concrete list of moral exchanges includes language about uncleanness and unchaste ways. These were retained as real categories of sin, but expressed broadly enough to include impurity of heart and conduct without narrowing the prayer to one sexual sin only.
significant_interpretive_choices: “The Beloved’s arms” was rendered as being held close to God’s beloved Son, interpreting the title as a reference to Christ rather than as a general image of divine affection.
“His death for my life” was interpreted as Christ’s death answering for the life forfeited by sin, not as a rejection of earthly life itself.

The many paired contrasts in the original were preserved as a single sustained gospel plea, because the accumulation is part of the prayer’s force: every aspect of the believer’s guilt is answered by the sufficiency of Christ.
